newsitem.title: UK: BOXING-HAMED LOOKS FOR QUICK WIN TO SILENCE U.S. CRITICS.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-HAMED LOOKS FOR QUICK WIN TO SILENCE U.S. CRITICS.

text.p: featherweight Naseem Hamed faces American Tom Johnson on a multiple world title bill on Saturday knowing that an impressive victory may finally pave the way to fame and fortune across the Atlantic.
The Sheffield fighter who likes to be called "Prince" Naseem is already one of the most popular -- and richest -- boxers in Britain but his star has yet to rise in the United States.

On Saturday, he pits his World Boxing Organisation featherweight title against the International Boxing Federation crown of "Boom Boom" Johnson in a unification bout. Another all-action victory that has become Naseem's trademark may force the American clique that controls the sport to finally take notice.
Featherweights may not be the biggest draw in the ring world but Naseem has forced himself into the spotlight with a series of brilliant performances -- and outrageous comments.

Confident to the point of arrogance, Naseem provoked an unofficial warning from the British Boxing Board of Control for telling Johnson he would end up in a graveyard during Thursday's head-to-head press conference.
Board general secretary John Morris made it clear to the Naseem camp that any similar outburst would not be ignored.
On Friday, the two fighters hotted up again at the weigh-in and were held apart by their respective camps when Johnson lost his patience with Naseem's taunts.
The diminutive Naseem, weighing in just half a pound heavier, goaded the American, saying: "You're finished, you're finished."
If Johnson hits the canvas in the third as Naseem has predicted, it may be enough to convince critics there is more to him than fast hands and a big mouth.

American trainer Eddie Futch said Naseem was "very elusive but also very vulnerable to the body because of the way he pulls his head back". U.S. boxing magazine The Ring ranks the Briton only third behind Johnson and WBC champion Luisito Espinosa of the Philippines.
Naseem said: "I want to give a good impression to all those Americans who have been slagging me off. There's no way on earth they can't give me credit after this one."
After his last less-than-impressive victory over Manuel Medina, Naseem took up early morning running to complement the usual gym workout in a bid to up his fitness level.
The new regime should pay off against Johnson, who at 32 and 11 successful title defences, has faced criticism that he is past his prime.
But the American is a veteran of 48 fights and has never been floored, so Naseems's prediction of an early knockout looks like unfounded fighting talk.
On the same bill, indestructible Irishman Steve Collins is a 1-6 shot to retain his WBO super-middleweight title against Frederic Seillier of France.

Collins, who built a reputation as a man impossible to hurt after his double victories over Britons Nigel Benn and Chris Eubank, still yearns for a unification showdown with American Roy Jones but his relentless, grinding style may not prove attractive to American promoters.
In another super-middleweight title fight, this time for the WBC version, Briton Robin Reid faces a tough battle against gritty South African Giovanni Pretorius.
Local hope Micky Cantwell attempts to wrest the WBO light-flyweight title from the secure-looking grip of South African Jake Matala.
